reader_question: Is a biweekly mortgage payment worth it?
decision_gap: Bank calculators show the saving but rarely the fee drag or the free 1/12-extra alternative.
method: calculated: amortize monthly (r/12), biweekly half-payments (r/26, 26 a year), monthly + 1/12 extra; fees = setup + per-payment × biweekly payments

sources.text: standard fixed-rate payment formula P = B·r/(1−(1+r)^−n), shown on page

assumptions: servicer credits each half-payment when received
interest at APR ÷ 26 per two-week period

findings.label: calculated
findings.text: $300,000 at 6.5% over 30 years: monthly $1,896.20, $382,633 interest; biweekly pays off in about 24.2 years with $294,512 interest, saving $88,122; adding $158 (1/12) a month saves $87,256 and pays off in 290 months.

findings.label: calculated
findings.text: A $395 setup fee plus $2.50 per payment costs $1,965 over 628 payments; $9.95 per payment costs $6,249.

findings.label: calculated
findings.text: Shorter loans save less: $150,000 at 6% with 10 years left saves $5,717 and finishes 1 year sooner.

counterexample: At a 0% rate biweekly payments save no interest (they only finish sooner); a servicer that holds half-payments until a full payment builds up saves less than shown.
unknowns: each servicer's crediting practice and fees
would_change: A prepayment penalty, plan fees near the interest saved, a short remaining term, or higher-rate debt elsewhere.
medium: interactive tool — balance, rate and fees change the verdict

provenance.placement: introText paragraph 1 and section 'How the Biweekly Mortgage Calculator Works'
